\title{When Do Variational Quantum Circuits\\ Keep Federated Training Data Private?}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{AJ Barea}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Rochester Institute of Technology\\
Rochester, NY, USA\\
ajb6289@rit.edu}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Gradient matching can rebuild a federated client's input from its shared gradient. For
variational quantum circuits (VQCs) the literature disagrees on whether that attack works. We test it on simulated 4- and 8-qubit data re-uploading circuits,
against an attacker who knows the circuit and its parameters. In \RqOneAttacks{} attacks with exact gradients, every circuit with one
encoding layer and at least two trainable layers gave up its input on \Seeds{} of \Seeds{} seeds.
At 8 qubits and a fixed \ParamsTopLarge{} effective parameters, the input was recovered on
\RecByRepsLarge{} of \Seeds{} seeds for 1, 2, 4 and 8 encoding repetitions, the failures stuck in
local minima. With
\BudgetRestarts{} restarts instead of \Restarts, \BudgetOthersCount{} of the \BudgetCircuits{}
hardest 8-qubit circuits gave up the input on \BudgetOthersMin--\BudgetOthersMax{} seeds, and the
\BudgetHardestCircuit{} circuit on \BudgetHardestRecovered. At 100 shots per expectation value, the attack came within \CloseRad~rad on at most \ShotLowWithinLargeMax{} of
\Seeds{} seeds for every 8-qubit circuit. Batches gave up their inputs at up to \BatchLeakMaxRatio{} unknowns per effective
parameter and never from \BatchHeldMinRatio{} up. Against a label-free attack, hiding binary
labels lowered recovery (paired exact McNemar $p \LabelPooledPAll$). Of the \LabelKnownOnlyAll{}
seeds recovered only with labels, \LabelKnownOnlyTwo{} had two inputs per update. Training the client's circuit on \TrainedTasks{} benchmark tasks showed no overall change in
recovery (\TrainedOnlyBeforeAll{} seeds recovered only before training,
\TrainedOnlyAfterAll{} only after, $p \TrainedPooledPAll$). Fewer seeds were recovered after
training on low-frequency curves, a lead for further tests.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
federated learning, gradient inversion, variational quantum circuits, privacy
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
In federated learning (FL), clients train a shared model on their own data and send the server
gradients or weight updates instead of the data~\cite{mcmahan2017}. On classical neural networks
those gradients can be inverted. The server searches for an input whose gradient matches the one it
received, and it often recovers the training example~\cite{zhu2019,geiping2020}.

For VQCs used as the FL model, three papers from one group reach different conclusions. Kumar et
al.~\cite{kumar2023} argue that expressive encodings give VQCs inherent privacy, because the
gradient equations become high-degree trigonometric polynomials with exponentially many local
minima. Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025} reconstruct inputs numerically from 2- and
6-qubit VQCs that are ``sufficiently overparameterized''. Heredge et al.~\cite{heredge2025} prove
that properties which make a VQC trainable also let an attacker extract snapshots of the encoded
state. The three papers use three different definitions of overparameterization and three
different attacks. Only Papadopoulos et al.\ add noise to the shared gradient, as Gaussian noise;
none simulates the shot noise of a device that estimates it.

This report measures where the attack works on one controlled family of circuits. It asks five
questions:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{RQ1.} At a fixed parameter count, do encoding repetitions protect the input better
  than trainable layers (Section~\ref{sec:rq1})? A restart-budget experiment then asks whether
  the attacks that failed would succeed with more restarts (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
  \item \textbf{RQ2.} How does shot noise in the client's gradient change the attack
  (Section~\ref{sec:rq2})?
  \item \textbf{RQ3.} How many inputs must a batch hold before the gradient protects them
  (Section~\ref{sec:rq3})?
  \item \textbf{RQ4.} Does hiding the label protect the input (Section~\ref{sec:rq4})?
  \item \textbf{RQ5.} Does training the client's circuit change what its gradient reveals
  (Section~\ref{sec:rq5})?
\end{itemize}
All five use the same circuits, attack and outcome definitions, and every attack's raw result is
committed with an open-source JAX simulator checked against PennyLane
(\url{https://github.com/ajbarea/csci739-qfl-privacy}).

\section{Background and Related Work}
\subsection{Gradient Inversion in Federated Learning}
In the deep-leakage attack~\cite{zhu2019}, the server holds the model parameters $\theta$ and a
client's gradient $g = \nabla_\theta L(x, y;\theta)$. It minimizes
$\|\nabla_\theta L(\hat x, y; \theta) - g\|^2$ over a candidate input $\hat x$. This needs the
gradient of a gradient, which automatic differentiation provides. Geiping et
al.~\cite{geiping2020} showed the attack recovers high-resolution images from realistic networks
and that sharing averaged updates over several local steps does not prevent it.

\subsection{Variational Quantum Circuits and Data Re-uploading}
A VQC encodes a feature vector $x$ into rotation angles, applies trainable gates with parameters
$\theta$, and outputs an expectation value $f(x;\theta)$. Repeating the encoding $r$ times, with
trainable blocks in between, is data re-uploading~\cite{perezsalinas2020}. With single-qubit
Pauli-rotation encodings, $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial in each feature whose frequencies grow
with the number of repetitions~\cite{schuld2021}: $r$ repetitions give integer frequencies up to
$r$. Every trainable gate in our circuits is a Pauli rotation, so gradients follow from the parameter-shift
rule~\cite{schuld2019}, which is how a device would compute them.

\subsection{Competing Claims for VQCs}
\emph{Inherent privacy.} Kumar et al.~\cite{kumar2023} encode each feature on $m$ qubits with
exponentially spaced frequencies (a ``Fourier tower'' map), so the gradient has frequencies up to
$(5^m-1)/2$. For a single feature they count local minima of one gradient entry's matching loss
growing as $e^{1.48m}$. At $m = 3$, a 60-step ADAM attacker started from 10 random points in each
of 100 trials does no better than guessing. They
assume the worst case for the client: batch size 1, exact gradients, and a known label.

\emph{Numerical inversion.} Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025} attack 2- and 6-qubit
angle-encoded VQCs. The attacker estimates the matching loss's gradient in $\hat x$ by finite
differences, smoothed by an adaptive moving-average filter and optionally a Kalman filter. Over 10
attacks from different starting points, both variants recover the input (mean squared error
$\le 0.005$) every time with 2 inputs; with 6 inputs the moving-average variant succeeds on
40--50\% of attacks and the Kalman variant on 70--80\%. They call a model overparameterized when
its gradient gives a number of equations comparable to or larger than the number of unknowns.
Gaussian noise added to the shared gradient raised their inversion error.

\emph{Privacy versus trainability.} Heredge et al.~\cite{heredge2025} consider an observable that
lies in the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. They show that once the number of
parameters is at least $\dim\mathfrak g$, a linear system recovers a snapshot of the encoded state
in time polynomial in $\dim\mathfrak g$, which they call a weak privacy breach. The attack is
efficient only when the Lie algebra is polynomially large. Recovering $x$ itself needs further conditions on the
encoding. In their analysis, Kumar et al.'s circuits stay private only because their Lie algebra
is exponentially large, which also makes them untrainable.

Our encoding is linear re-uploading, not the Fourier tower. Its frequencies grow linearly in $r$,
so our results test the mechanism Kumar et al.\ propose (more frequencies, more local minima) on a
different encoding, not their construction.

\section{Threat Model}
The server is honest but curious. It follows the FL protocol and tries to learn the client's input
from what it sees. It knows the circuit architecture, the current parameters $\theta$ (it sent
them), the observable, the loss, and the label $y$. It observes one client's gradient for a single
training example. This matches Kumar et al.'s worst case for the client~\cite{kumar2023}. The
client's parameters are untrained, drawn uniformly from $[0, 2\pi)$. Four experiments change this
setting. In RQ2 the client estimates its gradient from finite measurement shots. In RQ3 the client sends the mean gradient over a batch of $B$ examples. In RQ4 the server
does not know the labels. In RQ5 the client has trained its parameters on a classification task.

\section{Method}
\subsection{Circuit}
On $N$ qubits, starting from $\ket{0}^{\otimes N}$, the circuit repeats the following $r$ times: encode feature $x_q$ as $R_Y(x_q)$ on
qubit $q$, then apply $\ell$ trainable blocks. Each block applies $R_Y$ and then $R_Z$ to every
qubit, each gate with its own parameter, followed by an open CNOT chain $0\to1\to\dots\to N-1$ ($N-1$ gates, no wrap-around). The output is
$f(x;\theta) = \tfrac1N\sum_q\braket{Z_q}$ and the client's loss is $(f - y)^2$, with $y = 1$
outside RQ4 and RQ5. A single-qubit observable would leave some inputs outside its light cone, so
they would never reach the gradient. The mean over all qubits avoids that, and a test checks it on
several circuit shapes.

The circuit has $2r\ell N$ parameters. The last block's $R_Z$ gates are followed only by CNOTs and
a $Z$-diagonal measurement, so they never change the output. We report the
$P_{\mathrm{eff}} = 2r\ell N - N$ \emph{effective} parameters, and a test confirms on several circuit
shapes that exactly these have nonzero gradient. Inputs are drawn uniformly from $[0,\pi)^N$.

\subsection{Simulator}
The attack differentiates through a gradient, so it needs second-order automatic differentiation.
In our feasibility spike, PennyLane~\cite{bergholm2018} with autograd took \SpikeSeconds~s for
\SpikeSeeds{} attacks of \SpikeRestarts{} restarts each on a \SpikeQubits-qubit circuit with
$r = \SpikeReps$ and $\ell = \SpikeLayers$. Compiling the PennyLane circuit with JAX unrolls every
gate, so the compiled program grows with circuit depth. We wrote a statevector simulator in
JAX~\cite{jax2018} that scans over repetitions and blocks, so it compiles once per circuit shape.
At \CompileQubits{} qubits its first call, which compiles, took at most \CompileMaxSeconds~s for
the \CompileShapes{} shapes on \CompileCpus{} logical CPUs. Tests pin its output probabilities and
gradients to PennyLane's \texttt{default.qubit} within \ReferenceTol.

\subsection{Attack}
The attacker minimizes
\[
  \mathcal L(\hat x) = \big\|\nabla_\theta (f(\hat x;\theta) - y)^2 - g\big\|_2^2
\]
with L-BFGS-B~\cite{byrd1995}, using the exact gradient $\nabla_{\hat x}\mathcal L$ from automatic
differentiation, for at most \MaxIter{} iterations and without bounds on $\hat x$. It starts from \Restarts{} points drawn
uniformly from $[0,\pi)^N$ and keeps the restart with the lowest $\mathcal L$, which is all an
attacker without the true input can do.

With a batch $X = (x_1,\dots,x_B)$ the client sends the mean gradient
$g = \frac1B\sum_i \nabla_\theta(f(x_i;\theta) - y_i)^2$. The attacker solves for all $B$ inputs
at once. The gradient does not reveal the order of the batch, so the reconstruction error is the
largest feature error under the best matching of reconstructed to true inputs (a bottleneck
assignment).

Without the labels, the attacker uses the structure of the squared loss: sample $i$ contributes
$c_i\nabla_\theta f(x_i;\theta)$ with an unknown weight $c_i = 2(f(x_i;\theta) - y_i)/B$. For a
candidate batch $\hat X$, let $J$ have rows $\nabla_\theta f(\hat x_i;\theta)$. The attacker takes
the best weights in closed form and minimizes
\[
  \mathcal L_{\bar y}(\hat X) = \min_{c\in\mathbb R^B} \big\|J^\top c - g\big\|_2^2,
\]
solving the $B\times B$ normal equations. A ridge of \RidgeScale{} times the mean of
$\|\nabla_\theta f(\hat x_i)\|^2$ keeps them solvable. For $B = 1$ the loss depends only on the
angle between the two gradients, as in the cosine matching of Geiping et al.~\cite{geiping2020}.
Clients in RQ4 draw each $y_i$ from $\{-1, +1\}$, and the same clients are attacked with the
labels known for comparison.

\subsection{Outcomes}
Each attack ends in one of four outcomes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Recovered}: every feature lies within \RecoveredRad~rad of the true input, measured
  modulo $2\pi$ because $R_Y(x+2\pi) = -R_Y(x)$ differs only by a global phase.
  \item \emph{Close}: not recovered, but every feature within \CloseRad~rad. At low shot counts an
  exact match is out of reach, and a close reconstruction still reveals the input to within that
  angle.
  \item \emph{Ambiguous}: an input further away that matches the gradient at least as well as the
  true one, $\mathcal L(\hat x) \le \mathcal L(x) + \ExplainsSlack\|g\|^2$. For an exact gradient
  $\mathcal L(x) = 0$, so this is a second exact preimage.
  \item \emph{Stuck}: an end point (a local minimum, or the iteration limit) that matches worse
  than the true input.
\end{itemize}
Under shot noise we also report the median reconstruction error. A paired comparison (labels
known or not, before or after training) uses the exact McNemar test on the seeds recovered under
one condition only. Each setting has its own clients, so a pooled test adds the settings'
discordant pairs; we treat the pooled test as primary and the per-setting tests as descriptive.
Every setting uses \Seeds{} seeds, each with its own input and parameters. Error bars on
recovered fractions are 95\% Wilson intervals.

\subsection{Shot Noise}
For RQ2 the client estimates its gradient as a device would. Each $\partial f/\partial\theta_j$
comes from the parameter-shift rule, and each of the $2P+1$ expectation values (including $f$
itself) is the mean of $S$ sampled measurements, so one gradient costs $(2P+1)S$ shots. The client
estimates all $P$ entries, including the $N$ whose exact value is zero; their noise adds a
constant to the attacker's loss. The attacker still matches with its noiseless model.

\subsection{Training}\label{sec:rq5-training}
For RQ5 the client trains its circuit before the attack, on two binary classification families
from Bowles et al.'s benchmark of small quantum models~\cite{bowles2024}. We generate them with
their procedure, margin, offset and noise at $N = 4$ and 8 features. Every seed uses the same dataset for a given task and size. \emph{Linearly separable} draws \BenchSamples{}
points uniformly from $[-1,1]^N$ outside a margin of $\BenchMargin N$ around the hyperplane normal
to $(1,\dots,1)$. \emph{Two curves} embeds two 1-d curves into $N$ dimensions with a Fourier series
of degree $D$, offset by $1/(2D)$, with noise \BenchNoise; we use $D = 2$ and $D = 10$. The degree
sets the frequency content of the target, which Kumar et al.\ found to change what training does
to privacy~\cite{kumar2023}. Each dataset is split \TrainPercent/\TestPercent{} into training and
test sets, and each feature is scaled to $[0,\pi]$ on the training set.

Labels are $y\in\{-1,+1\}$ and the circuit predicts $\operatorname{sign} f(x;\theta)$. The client
minimizes the mean of $(f - y)^2$ over its training set with full-batch
Adam~\cite{kingma2015}. The learning rate is the one of \LearningRates{} with the best mean
validation accuracy after \TrainSteps{} steps, over \TuningSeeds{} runs on a held-out
\ValidationPercent\% of the training set. Each seed trains from its own random $\theta$, and the
attacker sees the gradient of one training example, chosen by the seed, at steps \TrainedSteps.
The attacks on a seed start from the same points, and the label is known.

\section{Experiments and Results}
\subsection{RQ1: Encoding Repetitions Versus Trainable Layers}\label{sec:rq1}
We ran every $(r,\ell)$ with $r\ell\in\{1,2,4,8\}$ at 4 and 8 qubits: \RqOneShapes{} circuit
shapes and \RqOneAttacks{} attacks. Table~\ref{tab:rq1} gives the outcome counts and
Fig.~\ref{fig:map} plots the recovered fraction at a fixed parameter count.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/privacy-map.pdf}
\caption{Fraction of \Seeds{} seeds recovered against encoding repetitions $r$, with $\ell = $
product$/r$ trainable layers, so each line holds the effective parameter count fixed. Bars are 95\%
Wilson intervals.}
\label{fig:map}
\end{figure}

Three regimes appear:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Too few parameters: a different input with the same gradient.} With $r = \ell = 1$
  there are $N$ effective parameters for $N$ unknowns. The best restart reached an exact match on
  every seed, but on a different input in \SquareWrongSmall{} of \Seeds{} seeds at 4 qubits and
  \SquareWrongLarge{} of \Seeds{} at 8 qubits. Of the \SquareWrongSmall{} at 4 qubits,
  \SquareCloseSmall{} lay within \SquareCloseMaxErr~rad of the truth (``close'' in Table~\ref{tab:rq1}).
  Another restart did find the true input on \SquareOtherRestartSmall{} and
  \SquareOtherRestartLarge{} of those seeds, but both matched exactly, so the loss could not single
  it out.
  \item \textbf{One encoding layer, more trainable layers: recovered.} Every $1\times\ell$ circuit
  with $\ell\ge 2$ gave up its input on \Seeds{} of \Seeds{} seeds, at both sizes, from
  \ShallowMinParams{} to \ShallowMaxParams{} effective parameters.
  \item \textbf{More encoding repetitions: stuck.} At a fixed parameter count, moving layers from
  the trainable block into encoding repetitions never lowered the number of stuck attacks, and on
  every line of Fig.~\ref{fig:map} the largest $r$ was stuck on more seeds than $r = 1$. At 8 qubits and
  \ParamsTopLarge{} effective parameters the input was recovered on \RecByRepsLarge{} of \Seeds{}
  seeds for $r = 1, 2, 4, 8$. At 4 qubits and \ParamsTopSmall{} parameters the counts were
  \RecByRepsSmall. For every shape with $r\ge2$, more seeds were stuck at 8 qubits than at 4:
  $4\times1$, for example, was stuck on \StuckFourOneSmall{} of \Seeds{} seeds at 4 qubits and
  \StuckFourOneLarge{} at 8 qubits.
\end{itemize}
No attack with $r\ge2$ ended ambiguous or close: every failure there was stuck.

(Table~\ref{tab:budget}). The seeds generate the same input, parameters and starting points, so
the first \Restarts{} restarts of each run repeat the RQ1 attack, and they reproduce its counts
exactly.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{At 4 qubits, the attack came within \CloseRad~rad on at least half the seeds at
  every shot count.} At 100 shots the median
  error was \ShotLowErrSmallMin--\ShotLowErrSmallMax~rad, with
  \ShotLowWithinSmallMin--\ShotLowWithinSmallMax{} of \Seeds{} seeds within \CloseRad~rad.
  \item \textbf{At 8 qubits, 100 shots stopped the attack on most seeds of every circuit}, with
  median errors of
  \ShotLowErrLargeMin--\ShotLowErrLargeMax~rad and at most \ShotLowWithinLargeMax{} seed of
  \Seeds{} within \CloseRad~rad. At \ShotWideAllAt{} shots the $1\times4$ circuit was back to
  \Seeds{} of \Seeds{} seeds within \CloseRad~rad.
  \item \textbf{At 8 qubits and 100 shots the noise was as large as the signal.} The median
  squared norm of the noise in the client's gradient was \ShotNoiseLarge, against \ShotSignalLarge{}
  for the exact gradient; at 4 qubits these were \ShotNoiseSmall{} and \ShotSignalSmall. Most
  8-qubit failures at 100 shots were ambiguous
  (\ShotLowAmbigLargeMin--\ShotLowAmbigLargeMax{} of \Seeds{} seeds): another input fit the noisy
  gradient as well as the true one. The exact gradient's squared norm fell from \ShotSignalSmall{} to
  \ShotSignalLarge{} between 4 and 8 qubits, consistent with gradients concentrating as random
  circuits grow~\cite{mcclean2018}; two sizes cannot show that trend.
  \item \textbf{Below \CloseRad~rad, the error fell about as fast as the shot noise.} We fit log median
  error against $\log S$ on the \ShotSlopeCircuits{} circuits whose median error was within
  \CloseRad~rad at three or more shot counts, using only those counts. The slopes ran from
  \ShotSlopeMin{} to \ShotSlopeMax; the standard error of $S$ samples has slope $-1/2$.
  \item \textbf{Noise moved few stuck seeds.} The 4-qubit $4\times1$ circuit was stuck on the same
  \StuckFourOneSmall{} seeds with exact gradients and at every shot count, from the same starting
  points. From \ShotDeepStuckFrom{} shots up, where no seed was ambiguous, the 8-qubit $4\times1$
  circuit was stuck on \ShotDeepStuckMin--\ShotDeepStuckMax{} of \Seeds{} seeds, against
  \StuckFourOneLarge{} with exact gradients; \ShotDeepStillStuck{} of those \StuckFourOneLarge{}
  were stuck at every one of these shot counts. These failures come mostly from the loss
  landscape, not from the noise.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{RQ3: Batch Size}\label{sec:rq3}
A batch of $B$ inputs gives the attacker $NB$ unknowns against the same $P_{\mathrm{eff}}$ gradient
entries. We attacked the $1\times2$ and $1\times4$ circuits at 4 and 8 qubits with
$B \in \{2, 4, 8\}$, exact gradients, the label $y = 1$ known, and \Restarts{} restarts. The
$B = 1$ rows are the RQ1 attacks (Table~\ref{tab:rq3}, Fig.~\ref{fig:batch}).

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Recovery stopped between \BatchLeakMaxRatio{} and \BatchHeldMinRatio{} unknowns per
  effective parameter.} Every circuit recovered the input on at least \BatchFewestRecoveredBelow{}
  of \Seeds{} seeds up to $NB/P_{\mathrm{eff}} = \BatchLeakMaxRatio$, and on none from
  \BatchHeldMinRatio{} up. No batch size in the grid lands on a ratio of 1, so the data bracket the
  crossover. Past $NB = P_{\mathrm{eff}}$ the gradient gives fewer equations than unknowns, so its
  exact preimages generically form a set of dimension at least $NB - P_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and
  ambiguity is expected. At equality, the $r = \ell = 1$ circuits of RQ1 already had other exact
  preimages. By our reading, Papadopoulos et al.'s threshold~\cite{papadopoulos2025} counts all
  $P$ parameters rather than $P_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Past that point every seed was ambiguous.} The attacker found a different batch that
  fits the gradient as well as the true one, with its worst-matched input a median of
  \BatchAmbigErrLow{} to \BatchAmbigErrHigh~rad from the truth.
  \item \textbf{Below it, the \BatchStuckQubits-qubit failures were stuck.} The
  \BatchStuckShallowCircuit{} circuit was stuck on \BatchStuckShallow{} seeds at
  $B = \BatchStuckShallowAt$, and the \BatchStuckDeepCircuit{} circuit on \BatchStuckDeep{} seeds at
  $B = \BatchStuckDeepAt$. More unknowns made the search harder before they made the answer
  ambiguous.
\end{itemize}

  tests). This is one dataset with one training example per seed, so we read it as a lead for further tests, not a result.
  \item \textbf{Every failure was stuck.} None of the \TrainedAttacks{} attacks ended close or
  ambiguous. Where recovery moved, it moved through stuck searches; the attack found no second
  exact preimage of a trained gradient.

  baseline, and on the linear task the 8-qubit $4\times1$ circuit fell
  furthest below it (Table~\ref{tab:rq5}). Privacy at step \TrainedFinalStep{} therefore describes
  partly trained circuits on some tasks.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\emph{What the regimes say about each claim.} Encoding repetitions made the attack harder at a fixed
parameter count, which points the same way as Kumar et al.'s mechanism~\cite{kumar2023}: more
encoding frequencies, more spurious minima. Our attacker runs L-BFGS-B for up to \MaxIter{}
iterations from \Restarts{} starts, solving for all features jointly; theirs runs 60 ADAM steps
from 10 starts on one feature. With a single input, the $1\times\ell$ results agree with
Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025}: once the trainable block gave more gradient equations
than unknowns, the attack succeeded on every seed. With batches at 8 qubits, some seeds got stuck
below that point (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).

\emph{Stuck is not private.} A stuck attack failed with this budget, from these starting points. It
does not show that the input is safe. With \BudgetRestarts{} restarts instead of \Restarts, most
stuck seeds gave up their input (Section~\ref{sec:budget}). On these circuits, encoding repetitions
behave like a work factor for the attacker. Kumar et al.'s minima grow exponentially in $m$
because their frequencies grow as $5^m$~\cite{kumar2023}. Ours grow linearly in $r$, so their
mechanism predicts slower growth in $r$ here. Whether the work factor grows exponentially with the
number of qubits, our two sizes cannot test.

\emph{Limitations.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item All circuits are simulated and at most 8 qubits. The results show where each claim holds
  at this size, not how it scales.
  \item RQ5 trains with one optimizer on \TrainedTasks{} small tasks, and the trained circuits fit
  some tasks poorly. The attack sees one training example's gradient per seed. In Kumar et al.,
  a model with 2 qubits per feature trained on a low-frequency target had a simpler attack loss landscape
  and less privacy, while one with 4 qubits per feature kept its privacy~\cite{kumar2023}. Our low-frequency lead points the other way, toward fewer recoveries
  after training, and the setups differ.
  \item A batch's error is that of its worst-matched input. We did not measure how many inputs of
  an ambiguous batch were still recovered.
  \item The attacker ignores the input domain. Inputs lie in $[0,\pi)^N$, so a domain-aware
  attacker could reject some ambiguous preimages; the results do not store reconstructed inputs,
  so we cannot count how many lie inside it.
  \item Shot noise is the only device noise modelled. Gate and readout noise are future work.
  \item We do not measure trainability, which Heredge et al.\ tie to the same structure that
  enables the attack~\cite{heredge2025}. We also did not compute our circuits' Lie algebras, so we
  cannot say whether their linear attack applies here.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
On simulated 4- and 8-qubit re-uploading circuits, against an attacker who knows the circuit and its
parameters, we asked when the attack fails on most seeds.

With exact gradients, the attack failed on most seeds in two cases. In the $1\times1$ circuits,
with exactly as many effective parameters as inputs, the gradient had several exact preimages.
Against the 8-qubit
\BudgetHardestCircuit{} circuit the attack found the input on \BudgetHardestRate\% of restarts,
and it failed on \BudgetHardestHeld{} of \Seeds{} seeds after \BudgetRestarts{} restarts. Every other circuit leaked its input on most seeds within \Restarts{} restarts, or within
\BudgetRestarts{} for the other circuits we retested. Moving parameters into encoding repetitions
made each restart less likely to succeed, pooled over seeds.

Under shot noise we ran \Restarts{} restarts and counted a reconstruction within \CloseRad~rad as a
leak. At 8 qubits and 100 shots per expectation value, the input leaked on fewer than half
the seeds of every circuit; at 1000 shots this held for \ShotPrivateAtSecond. The attack on the 8-qubit $4\times1$ circuit came within \CloseRad~rad on
fewer than half the seeds at every shot count. Without noise, \BudgetRestarts{} restarts
recovered it on most seeds, and we did not run \BudgetRestarts{} restarts under noise. At 4 qubits every circuit leaked on at least
half the seeds at every shot count we tried.

From \BatchHeldMinRatio{} unknowns per effective parameter up, no batch was fully recovered:
every attack found a different batch that fit the gradient as well as the true one. Up to
\BatchLeakMaxRatio, a larger batch left more 8-qubit attacks stuck at \Restarts{} restarts. Against
a label-free attack, hiding binary labels lowered recovery (pooled exact McNemar
$p \LabelPooledPAll$), \LabelKnownOnlyTwo{} of the \LabelKnownOnlyAll{} affected seeds in batches of
two and \LabelKnownOnlyTop{} on one circuit. An attacker that tries every labeling can include the
known-label attack for $2^B$ times the restarts.

Training the client's circuit showed no overall change in recovery (pooled exact McNemar
$p \TrainedPooledPAll$). The $1\times4$ circuits stayed mostly recoverable, and every failure was
stuck. Fewer seeds were recovered after training on low-frequency curves, a lead to test rather than a
finding.

Whether a client can still train on gradients as noisy as 100 shots, and whether the attacker's cost
grows exponentially with the number of qubits, are the questions this setup leaves open.
